narrative_story:
# Perdition Gulch

## I.

Five chairs faced the table. One body sat among them.

The meeting house had been built from clapboard and argument in the spring of 1867, when the town still believed itself to be a town. The planks had since warped to the color of old teeth. Dust lay on the table in a sheet so uniform it might have been applied by a craftsman, and on each of the four empty chairs the dust had taken on the particular quality of its surface, so that each absence was a specific absence, each emptiness inhabited.

The chair nearest the door had a scorch mark on its left arm where someone had once set down a pipe and forgotten it, or had not forgotten it but had wanted to see whether the wood would hold. The burn was the perfect oval of a closed eye. Beside it, the second chair sat lower than the others—its legs had been sawn down by two inches so that a child could sit with his feet near the floor, and the cutting had been done unevenly, so the chair rocked if you touched it, which no one now did. The third chair had grooves whittled along the back rail, not decorative but mnemonic, a language of notches no one else had ever been asked to read. The fourth chair, identical in construction to the one that was occupied, had a faint brownish watermark on its seat cushion, the kind of stain that could have been anything and that the woman sitting in the fifth chair knew to be blood.

Mirren sat with her boots flat on the floor and her spine against the slats. Through the window, which had cracked along its length during the second year of the drought, she could see Main Street in the condition the street had chosen for itself. A man she did not recognize was carrying bolts of cloth from the general store to a mule that did not belong to him. He moved without urgency. There was no one to hurry from. Across the street a bay horse, still saddled, stood where it had been left tied to a post that was no longer standing—the post had sagged into the dirt, and the horse had not understood that it was free, or had understood and chosen not to move, which was a kind of freedom too. A shutter banged once, twice, and then the wind died and the shutter hung open like a jaw.

Mirren raised both hands and pressed her palms against her temples.

It was a gesture she had been performing since before she could remember performing it. In childhood it had looked like a headache. In adolescence it had looked like exasperation. What it was, what it had always been, was a call—a touching of the walls of the room she shared with her sister, the interior room that had no analogue in architecture, that existed only in the twinned electrical fact of their two skulls. She pressed, and the press was a knock, and the knock expected an answer: the warmth of a second attention, a presence that did not arrive through the ears or the eyes but through some corridor behind both, the way light enters a house not through the window but through the crack beneath the door.

Nothing.

She pressed harder. The meat of her palms whitened against bone.

Nothing. The room behind the door was empty. The door was not even a door anymore. It was a wall that remembered having been a door, which was worse.

Outside, the man with the cloth finished loading the mule and led it south. The horse stayed. The shutter hung. The narrator of this account—if narrator is what we must call the thing that watches from the vantage of the landscape itself, from the patience of the alkali flats and the long memory of the creek that no longer ran—the narrator had seen the five chairs full. Had seen what fullness meant and what it did and what it cost. The narrator was in no hurry. Dust does not hurry. The settling of fine particulate upon a surface that will not be disturbed is the slowest act of burial available to the physical world, and the narrator understood burial, having presided over so many, having said nothing at each one.

Five chairs. Four empty. The dust continued its work.

---

## II.

Three years before the empty chairs, which is to say three years before the end, the five were still five.

They learned the Colter Gang was coming the way they learned most things: through the boy. Ephraim was nine years old and had not spoken voluntarily to anyone outside the five since the age of four, when he had told the barber, Mr. Howell, that Mr. Howell was thinking about his dead wife's hands and that the thinking was making Mr. Howell want to put down the scissors and walk into the desert and keep walking. Mr. Howell had set the scissors on the counter with great care and asked Ephraim's mother to leave the shop. Ephraim's mother was two years dead by the evening in question, and Ephraim was standing on the general-store porch with his fingers hooked into his suspenders, his head tilted at the angle of a dog hearing a pitch above the human register.

"Riders," he said. "Six. They want the stock pens. They're going to burn McAllen's barn because one of them—the one with the bay mare, he has a scar on his—it doesn't matter. They hate McAllen. They're coming up the eastern ridge because the one in front, the smart one, he remembers the draw from last autumn."

He said this to Luzia, who stood behind him in the shadow of the porch awning with her arms crossed and her eyes closed. She did not need her eyes for what she was doing. She was looking at the eastern ridge, or more precisely she was looking at the eastern ridge as it had appeared to her at eleven minutes past four in the afternoon on a Tuesday in March, six months earlier, when she had ridden to the top on an errand for salt and had paused and had glanced—only glanced, one sweep of the gaze, habitual and unpurposed—at the country below. That glance was still alive in her. Every glance she had ever made was still alive in her, the full fidelity of every photon that had struck her retina stored in some architecture of recollection too vast and too meticulous to call memory. Memory was what other people had. What Luzia had was a museum without walls.

"The draw funnels through a granite choke seventy yards wide," she said, her eyes still closed. "Loose scree on the north side—horses won't like it. The south side has juniper cover up to forty yards from the road. If they come single file through the choke, which they will because the smart one values control, the last rider won't clear the granite for ninety seconds after the first."

"Ninety seconds," Mirren said. She was standing at the southern end of the street. She was also, in the way that mattered, standing at the northern end of the street, because Cora was there, and Cora's eyes were Mirren's eyes, and the town lay between them like a length of rope held at both ends.

"Ninety seconds is enough," Cora said, at the northern end, and Mirren heard it in her own skull before the sound crossed the distance between them, the way you hear your own voice before it leaves your mouth.

Dutton was already walking to the center of the road.

He was a large man, not tall but dense, built like a stump that had been asked to wear a shirt, and he walked the way such men walk when they are not afraid—slowly, with the particular economy of someone who knows his body is not at risk. He carried no weapon. He stopped in the road's center and stood with his hands at his sides. The last of the light was on the ridge. Somewhere beyond it, six men and their horses were entering the draw.

What happened next happened in overlapping sequence, the way the sections of an orchestra enter a passage not simultaneously but in structured succession, each carrying the others' sound forward. Ephraim tracked the riders' thoughts through the draw—he could feel the smart one's confidence narrowing, could feel the one with the grudge against McAllen rehearsing the pleasure of fire, could feel the others' lesser minds following in formation like geese in a wake. He whispered distance estimates to Luzia. Luzia converted them against her map. The twins adjusted—Mirren drifting east toward the livery stable, Cora moving to the low wall behind the smithy—not through discussion but through the shared processing of a single tactical mind distributed across two bodies, the way a bird adjusts both wings without deciding to adjust either one.

The Colter Gang cleared the ridge and saw a town in its ordinary evening posture. Storefronts dark. One street. One man in the road, unarmed and still.

They did not see the child on the porch who was reading their intentions with the fidelity of printed text. They did not see the woman behind the awning whose eyes were closed because she was seeing more with them closed than they could see with theirs open. They did not see the two women at opposite ends of town who were, in the way that mattered, a single woman in two places, which meant that every angle was covered and every escape was sealed and the topology of the town had become, without any visible change, a trap.

What the smart one in front saw was the man in the road. What he felt—Ephraim would report this afterward, with the flat precision of a child who does not yet understand that other people's fear is not data—was a sudden deep wrongness, the wrongness of a landscape that is exactly as it should be and is therefore exactly wrong, the way a perfectly set table in an empty house is not an invitation but a warning.

The smart one pulled up. The others pulled up behind him.

For eleven seconds no one moved.

Then the smart one turned his horse. The others followed. They rode back through the draw and did not return to Perdition Gulch. Some of them never understood why. The smart one understood, or nearly did: he understood that the town had known he was coming, though he could not have said how, and he understood that the man in the road was not brave but something worse than brave—certain—and certainty in an unarmed man is a phenomenon that even violent men find unnavigable.

The five met in the meeting house afterward. Ephraim sat in his low-cut chair and swung his legs. Dutton poured water. The twins sat in their adjacent chairs and for some time did not need to speak aloud because they were debriefing internally, running the engagement back and forth between two minds like thread through a needle. Luzia opened her journal and began to notch the spine of her chair with a knife—a new mark, another night encoded—and her hand was steady and her face was the face of someone who has just done the thing she was made to do.

Outside, the townspeople of Perdition Gulch went to bed without knowing that anything had happened. There had been riders on the ridge at dusk, someone mentioned. Probably passing through. Wasn't that Dutton standing in the road? Odd man. Always was.

---

## III.

In the present—the slow, depopulating present of the empty chairs—Dutton was repairing the meeting-house shutter.

The hinge had rusted through during the spring rains that had not been spring rains so much as a single afternoon of drizzle followed by seven more months of the drought that had become the town's permanent weather, its climate of collapse. The shutter hung at an angle that bothered him. Most things that could be fixed bothered him when they were not fixed, a trait that in a man whose body repaired itself as automatically as other men breathe had the quality not of conscientiousness but of compulsion—a fidelity to wholeness that was, in hindsight, the outward expression of a power whose inward mechanism he had never chosen and did not fully understand.

He pulled the hinge pin. The shutter swung free. He caught it with his left hand, and as he did, the exposed head of a nail protruding from the frame raked across his right forearm. The motion was small. The nail was old and dark. The cut was two inches long, shallow, clean, the kind of wound that in his experience—and his experience of his own wounds was vast and entirely monotonous—would seal itself before the blood had time to run past the wrist.

He looked at it.

The blood ran past the wrist.

He set the shutter down. He held his forearm out in front of him and looked at the cut the way you look at a clock whose hands have stopped and you are not sure whether to trust the silence or the memory of ticking.

The blood continued. Not much of it—the cut was shallow—but continuously, with the steady seep of a thing that intended to continue.

He stood on the porch for ten minutes.

Ten minutes is not a long time. Ten minutes is the time it takes to boil an egg, to saddle a horse if the horse cooperates, to walk from the meeting house to the creek bed and discover again that the creek has not returned. But ten minutes spent watching your own blood emerge from a wound that should not still be a wound is not ten minutes. It is a corridor. It is a corridor with no doors and a slight downward grade, and the light at the far end is not an exit but a window onto a further corridor, and the grade continues, and the light narrows, and the ten minutes pass in the manner of ten hours observed from inside a body that has just learned, for the first time in its life, that it is a body.

The blood slowed. Not because the power returned, but because blood slows. Because the clumsy, animal, unmiraculous machinery that every other human being relies upon—the platelets, the fibrin, the ordinary clotting that Dutton had not needed since he was eleven years old—stirred itself like a broken-down horse asked one more time to stand.

He wrapped the cut with a rag from his back pocket. The rag was gray. The blood darkened it to black.

He said nothing.

He went inside. He sat in his chair—the one with no distinguishing marks, which was itself a mark, the absence of idiosyncrasy the signature of a man who had never needed to fidget, to smoke, to carve his worry into the wood, because his body had never given him anything to worry about. He sat with his forearm in his lap and the rag around it and he attended the evening meeting when the others arrived, and he listened to Luzia report on the supply situation and he listened to the twins discuss the Garrett family's departure by wagon that morning and he listened to Ephraim say, with the discomfort of an adolescent who can hear everything and wishes he could not, that the remaining townspeople were thinking about leaving, most of them, that their thoughts had the particular color of people who have already decided but have not yet admitted the decision to themselves.

Dutton listened to all of this with his forearm in his lap.

That night, in his quarters behind the dry-goods warehouse, he sat on the edge of his cot and unwound the rag.

The wound was closed. Barely. A thin, raised line, pink and new, the kind of scar a normal man would carry for a week before it faded. Dutton had never had a scar. The novelty of it—this faint seam in his skin, this record—was as alien to him as flight.

He looked at the scar with the expression of a man reading a letter he had hoped was a mistake.

It was not a mistake.

He wrapped the arm again, though the wrapping was no longer medically necessary. He lay back on the cot. He did not sleep. Outside, the wind moved what was left of the topsoil from one side of the street to the other, and in the meeting house the five chairs stood in their row, and the dust settled, and the narrator watched him not sleeping the way the desert watches a fire on its horizon—patiently, knowing what comes after the light goes out.

---

## IV.

This had happened before, or something like this had happened before—the convening, the crisis, the five chairs full and the candle between them throwing five shadows against the plank walls.

Seven years before the present
